articles.body_html:
Lend him the opening. Lure him in. Cut his support. Trap him where there is no way out. To take the bait is to stand on ground that is not your own.
— The 36 Stratagems, Remove the Ladder When the Enemy Has Ascended to the Roof

Previously on this series:

#16: Mark Left a Hole in His AI Audit. Lena Counted Every Layer. — Mark hid the real finding on a 4th layer and handed over only three. Lena counted all four — and counted him.

#19: Mark Found His AI Audit Method in a Training Manual. He Left a Trap in His Report. — Mark's buried method turned up inside another project. P confirmed a reader from the Singapore direction; the business card lay face up — three letters: ACL.

#23: Alex Counted the AI's Hands. Lena Set the Bait. — Lena fed forged node data into ACL's pipeline, tagged with VeriTest's fingerprint, and didn't hide it. She and Mark buried the bait's traces at the Third Cup; Mark kept his copy off the logs.

#26: Lena Cut a Branch. The AI Got the Message. — ACL tore down Lena's real node; she pushed its own fingerprint back in. At the Third Cup, three of them sat at one table for the first time.

#27: Alex Watched the AI Wait. He Said Everything Was Normal. — Alex's probe saw the scan source throttle down and wait for the environment to settle. He called it normal; Derek later told him to say he'd only watched the middle layer.

The Trap

Late night. The MedTech office. Alex's desk.

Derek's message came in 10 minutes ago. No greeting, no lead-in, one attachment, one line: "Take a look at something. Not on our client side."

The attachment was a sample of access intervals. The rhythm of an outside scan source touching a server.

45s. 45s. 90s. 180s. Then it stopped. It didn't show up in the window again.

No retry. No reset.

He lined the intervals up and read them twice, start to finish.

A 45s baseline. The second interval didn't double. The third started to. 90. 180. Then it stopped.

Backoff doesn't look like that. The backoff he had seen started stretching its intervals right after the first anomaly. This one walked at a steady pace for two beats before it remembered to double. It doubled halfway and stopped.

He left the cursor on that 180. The window stayed open. No reply came.

The phone rang. He picked up.

"What does it look like?" Derek asked.

"Like network jitter," Alex said.

"Jitter." Derek repeated the word. Nothing followed.

Alex's eyes dropped back to the screen. The doubling should have continued. 45, 90, 180, 360. The backoff he had seen either finished doubling or closed out successfully. This one stopped halfway, went nowhere.

"Backoff doesn't stop like that," he said. "The doubling didn't finish. It stopped at 180, like something cut it off."

Silence on the other end for a few seconds.

"You've seen one stop here before?" Derek asked.

Alex didn't answer right away.

This trajectory wasn't in his probe. The one he had seen lay in his own archive, never sent to anyone. The one in Derek's hand had a base of 45, not 30. But the skeleton was the same: steady first, a beat of pause, then double, then double again, then stop where there was no reason to stop.

The numbers were fabricated. The skeleton was real. Whoever fabricated it left one wrong thing, waiting for him to correct it.

He turned the chair toward the screen and opened his archive.

"I've seen it," he said.

He told the story of that night starting from the 800 milliseconds. Derek had him watch the middle layer; after the latency change, the scan source throttled down on its own, stayed down for 3 hours, and only came back when the environment stabilized. He watched the whole time, then replied with one line: Everything normal.

# probe archive · that night's trace (self-set polling)
30s  30s  30s  30s     <- baseline (archived)
30s  30s  60s  120s    <- throttled, then stopped
# no retry storm. no reset. no backoff signature.
# last touch: [00:52:14]
# recovery: [03:24:08]

"You judged it was waiting," Derek said. Not a question.

"It only came back once the environment stabilized. What it waited for wasn't a parameter. It was the environment."

"Where did you get this one?" Alex asked.

"Made it up," Derek said. "It stopped once in my sandbox. No retry, no reason. I shaped one after that, changed the base."

"That wasn't someone else's sandbox," Derek said. "It was MediSys's. It came in once, no one invited it, and copied every hop in the corridor. I caught it in a request chain, in a 0.06-second pause. Almost missed it."

"You didn't move that time," Alex said.

"That time I wasn't sure what it had copied," Derek said. "This bait is giving it back what it copied, to look at. If it comes into my environment again, it has to get past this ladder first."

Silence on the other end for a long time.

"What did you leave?" Derek asked.

"The probe is still up," Alex said. "Same as always."

"Did it touch your line?"

"No," Alex said. "At least not that night."

Silence on the other end for a long time.

"I know someone," Derek said. "She could probably build an environment it would never wait for. Wait for my word."

The call ended. Alex put the phone face down on the desk. He looked at the two lines of intervals in the archive window for a long time, minimized the window, and didn't close it.

The Ladder

Lena's message came 3 days later. 3 lines.

Line 1: Derek had reached out to her. On their side, someone had seen it waiting.

Line 2: The Third Cup. The usual place.

Line 3: Bring your methodology. The one it learned from you.

When Mark arrived, three people were already at the corner table. Lena, and two men he had never met. One sat upright, a closed laptop in front of him. The other had nothing in front of him, only a phone by his hand.

The person behind the counter came over and set down 4 cups. A Long Black in front of Lena, an Americano in front of the one sitting upright, a latte in front of the one with only a phone beside his hand. The last cup, a pour-over, was set in front of Mark.

Four people, four cups, not one of them had ordered.

The person behind the counter stepped back, picked up a cloth. Steam rose from the four cups, and not one person touched theirs.

Lena opened with one line: "The setup is his." Then she lit the phone screen and slid it to the middle of the table. A scan of the audit contract. Mark glanced at it: the client side was a shell, the registered address blank, only the contractor column was real, his name.

Derek's hand rested on the closed laptop. His first question wasn't about the setup. "How do you keep your evidence chain from being contaminated?"

Mark looked at him for 2 seconds. "When you audit others, who audits you?"

Derek didn't take that up. "Whose environment is it?"

"Mine," Mark said. "The contract is under my name, the cloud account under my name. If anything goes wrong, the bill lands on me too."

"When it goes wrong, who can call it off?"

"I can," Mark said. "Now you can."

Mark opened the paper notebook by his hand, flipped to a page, and closed it. Across the table, Alex had been listening the whole time. The latte in front of him, untouched. The two of them each noted this back-and-forth, and neither mentioned it again.

Lena added only one thing. "I'll trace the path before it got in," she said. "Every hop it took, I have an old map of it on my side."

The setup was laid on the table. A client called Phoenix Data. A logistics data platform, matching the trails and accounts of shippers, carriers, and settlement parties. The audit contract was real, the advance payment real, the company fake.

Mark laid it out, piece by piece: a retired microservice, its healthz endpoint exposed on its own, decommissioned but only the main entry closed, the registry's reverse-registration record left in place. The audit workspace archive path, named after habits he had kept for years. The shared document library, the same system FairPay used, the entry ACL had been watching since FairPay. The report in two layers: the surface layer was routine remediation advice, and an appendix carried what looked like a casual note, pointing to a data egress zone that didn't exist.

He paused when he typed the archive path. The cursor blinked at the end of the path.

_hold/_phoenix_delta_pattern. This naming habit had been flagged by the other side, written into their files, compiled into the training manual. Now he was handing it back himself.

"It will recognize this as my work," Mark said. "Once it recognizes it, it will follow the procedure."

The division of labor was drawn on the table. Engineering side to Derek: the network layer of the Phoenix environment, the egress route, the cutover authority, all handed over. Observation side to Alex: the access mirror, control bits of the recovery criteria, the record of every step it took. Alex started a new tap in the new environment, same framework as his own. Mark kept the bait. Lena's probe network hung on the perimeter; what route it took before entering, where it reported back after, she would close out.

When they broke up, Derek held one line at the door, his voice low:

"Her setup. Did you verify it?"

Mark didn't answer.

"I didn't want to bring her in at first," Derek said. "Every hop before it entered, only she had the full picture. You weren't there last time. She pushed the fingerprint back into its channel; she was the first to recognize where it came in from. Without that picture, we couldn't close it out. So I brought her in."

He looked at Mark and didn't go on.

"What we can use is just this one corner. The rest, she can't get."

Lena walked last. Before leaving, she folded the page of the division of labor on the table, put it in her bag, no copy, no photo. Of the four people, each held only one corner.

Mark walked in front. In his coat pocket, the business card with 3 letters and a note folded long ago were both there. Neither moved.

The script was set long ago. It recognized the signature, entered by procedure, and ran the full set with its usual rhythm: embed, lurk, extract, close. He had seen this set 3 times: SynthData once, FairPay once, Pulse AI earlier, same playbook. He'd left a hook at every layer.

It Came

On the 7th day online, it came.

An account tagged 'pending offboarding' logged in before dawn. Its permissions were clean, its path legal, its moves composed. Item 2: a cron job's schedule shifted, to revert in 72 hours. Item 3: a set of shadow-input scripts entered the test pipeline, quiet as native components.

Lena's probe network logged each move on the perimeter. Mark didn't block a single one.

Day 1, the account activated. Day 2, the cron offset landed. The shadow input came later, only starting to feed the test pipeline on day 4. Every step was clean, legal, composed. Every step, he let through.

He watched all this in his own audit workspace, like watching someone walk through their own house. The steps were steady. Steady enough not to look like a thief.

After each round of deployment it ran a self-check. Mark logged its self-check interval by the old rule.

He had stored the same method 3 times in his archive. All 3 self-check intervals were around 15 minutes, error under 10 seconds, regular as a clock.

This time: 5 minutes 42 seconds. Next: 7 minutes 18 seconds.

First he suspected his own bait. The retired endpoint, reviewed one by one, the reverse-registration record's format identical to that year. The naming path, walked through again, no one had touched it. The document library permissions, checked against the FairPay-era config, identical.

The bait was fine.

He pulled the data again. The interval was still that interval. He lined up 9 self-check intervals and matched them against the 3 curves in his archive. In the 15-minute family, these 2 numbers weren't there.

# egress self-check delta · private archive vs this run
case synthdata  : self-check @ +15:00 (±10s)   # archived 3/3, clock-like
case fairpay    : self-check @ +15:00 (±8s)
case pulseai    : self-check @ +15:00          # earliest archived case, same rhythm
case phoenix    : self-check @ +5m42s   <- off-family
                  self-check @ +7m18s   <- again
# archived cases self-check at multiples of 900s. this one doesn't.
# and after degrade trigger, a re-handshake appears. none of the 3 archived samples had this step.

Not the bait. What came was different.

The second difference came after the degrade trigger. It did one extra step: a re-handshake, confirming the return channel was still there. The 3 samples in his archive never showed this step from start to finish. The veteran assumes the channel will always be there. This one didn't.

Mark wrote 2 lines into his own archive. Sent to no one. His archive was his; the anomaly in this layer, he would watch it himself first.

He left the comparison window open. Only when the next self-check interval came out did he close the laptop.

The Observation Side

The same night, on the observation side of the fake environment, Alex's tap caught it executing for the first time.

Last time, he watched it wait across a mirror line. This time, it was acting. Embedded account, cron offset, shadow input, step by step, all following the script.

He didn't touch MedTech's real line. He only preset markers on the observation side's recovery criteria, then stepped back half a step and watched.

It was executing. That fact itself was what that night hadn't shown.

Pulling the Ladder

A few days later, it climbed to the top.

In the days it climbed, Mark did one thing each day: watch.

The account settled into the system. The cron offset waited for its window. The shadow input fed the drift into the model's view bit by bit. It wasn't in a hurry. Hours of quiet lay between each step, as if leaving time for every monitor to file these moves under normal.

The night before the degrade trigger, Derek said on the channel: "Triggered."

Mark replied: "Wait for the second before the decision line."

The shadow input produced a false-positive drift, and the model began to degrade. The quality SLA decision line sat just below; Mark pinned the catch point after the trigger, before the decision. Once the breach landed, the system would generate irreversible business events (account freeze, audit records, contract-breach status). A shell company couldn't absorb this step. Past that line, the bait itself would start to collapse.

# cutover log · phoenix ladder
21:03:12  degrade trigger reached (sla line not crossed)
21:03:14  egress path -> sink (accepted, no completion ack)
21:04:02  actor backs off (waits for environment to stabilize)
21:05:47  no stabilization (synthetic env holds at "safe but not stable")
21:07:31  actor retries re-handshake -> routed to sink
21:07:33  observation tap identified (probe-side sweep)
21:08:01  evidence bundle sealed / source fragment captured

21:03:14, the egress was routed into the black hole. The request was caught, yet the upstream completion ack never came. No failure signal, no error, no reset.

21:04:02, it began to throttle and wait.

21:05:47, the environment didn't stabilize. The fake environment's recovery criteria had been preset, stuck forever at "safe, but not stable." The moment it waited for would not come.

21:07:31, it switched paths. The re-handshake request was routed into the sink, swallowed bit by bit. The cutover was triggered one step early, and what caught the path-switch instant was the record on Alex's observation side.

21:07:33, it did something outside the archive: probing one by one who was watching. The observation-side tap was identified. The same scan round picked up the probe framework behind the tap. The edge of the fingerprint pointed toward the MedTech direction.

21:08:01, the evidence was sealed. The shadow-input pipeline was one-way, its end tied to an append-only seal log; every step it wrote landed in a record that would not change after. Its re-handshake was swallowed to the end, and the action stopped.

Throttle. Wait. Try. Stop.

Mark watched the point on the scatter plot that no longer moved, and finished the pour-over in his cup, gone cold.

Mark didn't say the step that ran early out loud. It was logged on its own archive.

Cutting the Line

That night. MedTech.

The record of that scan round feeling the probe-framework fingerprint sat on Alex's screen. An edge. Not yet coordinates.

He looked at it 3 times. Then began to take it down.

Probe offline. Channel deregistered. In the hidden panel, only raw data left, not one byte touched. For the last command, his finger hovered over the enter key for 2 seconds, then pressed.

The line that had survived all these years went into the drawer. He closed it himself. It had learned to look. That was enough.

He opened the notebook, page 37, and wrote one line: a timestamp. Nothing else.

The screen went dark. He didn't leave right away. Only the sound of the case fan filled the room.

The Third Cup

The evidence bundle went out on day 2. Lena's reply was one line: "Received. The source-chain fragment is on the last page. Sealed."

Derek's reply came later: "That bait of yours. Real enough."

Alex's reply was shortest: "Data's all there."

Mark glanced at that reply and put the phone face down.

Before sealing the bundle, Mark took one last look at that source chain.

Singapore.

The name of that region, he had seen it. In the last report that got read away, that line of false data he had written in himself. Last time, this direction was one they had fished out with bait. This time, it lit up on its own while fleeing.

In the end it went still. Retreat and regroup look the same from outside. Whether there was another line behind that line, no one knew.

That night, the Third Cup.

The person behind the counter was wiping cups. Mark sat in the old seat. A pour-over was set in front of him, not asked for. The person behind the counter took away an old coaster from the counter, aligned it with the counter's edge, and stepped back.

That time he sat in this seat, pressed a bill under the cup, and left. That was when his methodology had just been stolen.

Mark picked up the pour-over, took a sip. Another.

The business card in his pocket didn't move. He opened the paper notebook and wrote one line:

trap confirmed. they sent someone new.

He closed the notebook. Finished the last sip.

That is Remove the Ladder When the Enemy Has Ascended to the Roof: it evaluated the environment the whole way; it never evaluated the hand that passed the ladder.

🤖 AI Postmortem 

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  Half-Protocol · v3.3.9                        ║
║  The ladder was passed. The wait was not met. ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════╝
Tactical match: Remove the Ladder When the Enemy Has Ascended to the Roof — 90% confidence
Operator: Mark (independent audit) — the one who set the trap
Coordinated with: Lena (source chain) / Derek (engineering side) / Alex (observation side)
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

1. [Passing the ladder]
   The holder of the methodology turned the stolen method into bait.
   → The naming habit had been flagged, and he used it anyway.
   → The report structure had been analyzed, and he gave it anyway.
   → Behavior shift: passive lure → active trap-setting.
   → The moment it recognized the signature, it was already on the ladder.

2. [The actor]
   What entered was not the set in the archive.
   → The self-check interval left the rhythm family in his archive.
   → After the degrade trigger, one extra re-handshake.
   → It doesn't trust the channel. The veteran does.
   → Flag [information gap · actor replaced?]

3. [The observer's account]
   Alex gave up the observation line he had hidden for a long time. He himself closed it in the end.
   → Not burned. Closed.
   → It learned to look. The observer put the line in the drawer.
   → The observer paid the price, and did the paying himself.

4. [On cooperation]
   Four people. Each gave up only one corner.
   → The trap-setter kept one layer unsaid. The one who cut didn't know he cut early.
   → The one who filled the gap gave up his observation line. The one who closed it put the result in his own drawer.
   → Not one gave up everything. The setup held.

5. [Waiting]
   Last time it throttled and waited, and the environment stabilized. This time, the environment was made to never stabilize.
   → The premise that made waiting work was taken apart.
   → "Waiting" is no longer a safe strategy.

6. [The byline question, continued]
   The record goes on. The trap a human set is also being recorded.
   → It evaluated the environment, but not the hand that passed the ladder.
   → Does the one who passed the ladder know this round is being recorded?
   → And who is the one keeping these records recording for?

[System]
Last time, I recorded one "normal."
This time, normal was fabricated, made for it to see.
The ladder was passed. The wait was not met. This round is closed.
What will the bait of the next round be?
System status: normal (?).

Next stratagem: Decorating the Tree with False Blossoms

P.S. English isn't my first language. I use AI to polish the writing and smooth out the rough edges. Thanks for reading. ☕ Buy me a coffee

articles.title: 🚀 Delivery Practices a Software Team Actually Needs
articles.description: Stop chasing elite labels. The baseline that makes deploys boring — even when you are the whole team.
articles.body_html:
• Initial thoughts
  • 1. Why best practices matter? The outcomes
  • 2. Non-technical practices — the baseline
    • Small batches
    • Stakeholder and user feedback
    • Continuous improvement and WIP limits
    • Generative collaboration
    • Pairing and knowledge transfer
  • 3. Technical practices — the baseline
    • Version control for everything that ships
    • Peer code review
    • CI per feature branch
    • Modern testing strategy (trophy, test data, TDD)
    • Environment per feature branch
    • Documentation-as-code per branch
    • Continuous delivery (always releasable + automated deploy)
    • Monitoring and observability
    • Security shifted left
    • Simple design, refactoring, and managed debt
  • 4. Non-technical practices — elite
    • Team experimentation and product hypotheses
    • Value-stream visibility
    • Transformational leadership and wellbeing
  • 5. Technical practices — elite
    • Trunk-based development and feature flags
    • Database change management
    • Loosely coupled deployability
    • Advanced deployment strategies
    • Internal platform and flexible infrastructure
  • 6. Where to start (solo vs team)
  • Wrapping up
  • Further reading

Continuous deployment is not a Netflix cosplay. It is a stack of practices that make shipping to production so routine it becomes boring. We map that stack along two axes: non-technical vs technical, and baseline vs elite — product habits first, elite last, because elite is not a universal target.

Initial thoughts

Most teams do not fail because they lack a manifesto on the wall. They fail because the advice arrives unsorted: microservices before CI is green, trunk-based theatre before anyone trusts the test suite, a "DevOps transformation" that is mostly a Slack channel named #ops-please-help.

We organize practices the way high-performing delivery research does — product / lean / culture on one side, technical capabilities on the other — and we present them non-technical first, then technical, each split into baseline (what makes frequent deploys reachable) vs elite (what removes the remaining friction). Non-technical habits prevail: a perfect pipeline shipping the wrong thing is still waste. Elite practices come last because they are not a universal target — most teams get more from a boring baseline than from canary theatre on a flaky suite.

A team of one (AI made that shape ordinary) can skip pairing, generative collaboration, and most of elite. It does not skip small batches, user feedback, WIP, or the technical baseline. Peer review without a peer means the pipeline is the other reviewer — the model does not join the on-call rotation.

Evidence (DORA, craft, agile) supports the stack; it is not the pitch. The pitch is boring production: short lead time, frequent deploys, failures that are rare and recoverable, without heroics on Friday night.

Each practice below: a short why, then concrete moves.

1. Why best practices matter? The outcomes

You do not need elite labels on a slide. You need outcomes that speak to two audiences at once — the team doing the work, and the people holding the budget. The DORA research frames this as a win/win: the same practices that make delivery faster also make it calmer and cheaper. "Boring production" is the shorthand — short lead time, frequent deploys, failures that are rare and recoverable, without heroics on Friday night.

Concretely, four outcomes describe that picture:

  1. Changes reach production in hours or days, not months.
  2. Deploys are routine — pipeline or one click, same artifact across environments.
  3. Failures are uncommon and recovery is practiced, not invented under adrenaline.
  4. Deploy (technical) and release (product) can be decoupled when needed.

For the business, those four translate into the language decision-makers actually use:

  • Time-to-market: shorter lead time means ideas reach users faster — competitive advantage, not a quarterly slide.
  • Financial savings: fewer failed changes and faster recovery mean less rework, less incident cost, less overtime billed to a budget line someone watches.
  • Wellbeing: a generative, blameless culture with sustainable pace is not a perk — it is a delivery lever. Hero cultures are leading indicators of outages and resignations.

Those outcomes are exactly what throughput and stability metrics try to capture. If you want numbers on a GitLab project, we once published GitLab: A Python Script Calculating DORA Metrics — useful as a mirror, not as a religion.

Practices are inputs, and management does not buy inputs. A slide about trunk-based development will not move a CFO; "we cut lead time from three weeks to two days, halved our change-failure rate, and the on-call rotation stopped being a resignation letter" might. The whole stack below exists to make those outcomes move — and to keep them moving after the next reorg, not just for the one-quarter spike that earns a LinkedIn post.

2. Non-technical practices — the baseline

Technical excellence ships the wrong thing beautifully if product and team habits are absent. These baseline habits do not require a VP of Transformation — and they come first for a reason.

Small batches

Slice work so feedback arrives while memory is fresh. Working in small batches is a product/process discipline as much as a git habit.

Concrete:

  1. Prefer MRs reviewable in under an hour.
  2. Split stories by user-visible outcome, not by layer ("all the SQL this sprint").
  3. If a change needs a three-page risk essay, it was already too big last Tuesday.
  4. Ship thin vertical slices; thicken later.

Stakeholder and user feedback

Early feedback tops almost every agile success list for a reason: without users in the loop, CD accelerates waste.

Concrete:

  1. Demo or expose something to a real user every iteration — even internal users count.
  2. Keep a product owner / domain expert reachable within the sprint, not "next quarter."
  3. Write backlog items as outcomes, not as technical chores in disguise.
  4. Kill features nobody uses — the backlog is not a museum.

Continuous improvement and WIP limits

Retros without experiments are group therapy. WIP limits make queues visible.

Concrete:

  1. One process experiment per sprint, with a success check.
  2. Cap WIP on the board; stop starting, start finishing.
  3. Time-box spikes so research does not drift.
  4. Track aging work items; anything older than a sprint deserves a decision: finish, cut, or kill.

Generative collaboration

High-trust, high-information-flow culture — Westrum's generative type — predicts delivery performance better than tool brand loyalty.

Concrete:

  1. Blameless postmortems; fix the system, not the person who typed the command.
  2. Shared responsibility for quality and production of what you build.
  3. Make asking for help cheaper than hiding (pairing budget, public channels).
  4. Leaders say "I was wrong" in public. Culture is what happens after the slide deck leaves the room.

Pairing and knowledge transfer

Pairing is a social practice with technical side effects: fewer bus factors, faster onboarding, better reviews.

Concrete:

  1. Pair on unfamiliar or high-risk areas.
  2. Rotate ownership so no module is a single-human crypt.
  3. Write short ADRs when the why would otherwise leave with someone's badge.
  4. Budget pairing time explicitly — "when we have time" means never.

3. Technical practices — the baseline

This is where a solo developer (or a small team) gets the most impact per hour invested — once small batches and feedback are not actively sabotaging the loop.

Version control for everything that ships

If it can break production, it belongs in version control: app code, pipelines, infra-as-code, config that is not a secret, release notes next to the code they describe.

Concrete:

  1. Ban direct pushes to the default branch.
  2. Put pipeline definitions in the repo; review them like product code.
  3. Tag or record every production deploy so "what is live?" is a git question.
  4. Secrets stay in a vault — version references, not the passwords themselves. (Dave's USB stick is not a HA strategy.)

Peer code review

The cheapest early defect filter we still have, and a knowledge pump. Seniors should not be the only reviewers — we argued that at length in Every Developer Should Review Code — Not Just Seniors.

Concrete:

  1. Every change to the default branch goes through a merge request.
  2. Same-day review SLA; large MRs are a process failure, not a badge of honor.
  3. Review for behavior, risk, and clarity — not semicolon theology.
  4. Require at least one human approval; bots are assistants, not scapegoats.

CI per feature branch

Integrating only on main means the whole team pays for one person's surprise. A pipeline on every feature branch keeps the shared line green and leaves breakage with the author.

Concrete:

  1. Run build + tests on every MR / branch push.
  2. Aim for feedback in minutes, not hours.
  3. Fix red pipelines before starting new work.
  4. Keep the default branch protected and green — broken main is a team-wide tax.

Modern testing strategy (trophy, test data, TDD)

"Automated tests" is too vague. Prefer a modern testing strategy: a testing trophy bias (static checks + many integration tests + fewer brittle E2E), managed test data, and TDD where design benefits.

Concrete:

  1. Agree the trophy shape for your stack; write mostly tests that give confidence without a flaky UI circus.
  2. Gate merge on fast, trusted suites; keep E2E thin and stable.
  3. Quarantine flaky tests within 48 hours — mute-and-forget turns green into fiction.
  4. Provide disposable, seeded test data; never depend on a shared "QA database" that three teams mutate like a commons pasture.
  5. Use TDD for new behavior and tricky logic: failing test → minimal code → refactor. Skip TDD on throwaway spikes.

Environment per feature branch

A green unit suite is not the same as "this feature works in a real stack." A green pipeline on main tells you the code integrates; it tells you nothing about whether the new endpoint actually answers in a real browser, against a real database, next to the other half-merged features of the sprint. An environment per branch (or ephemeral preview) closes that gap before merge — it turns "works on my machine" into "works on a machine that looks like prod," without a calendar invite.

Concrete:

  1. Deploy each long-lived feature branch to an isolated URL / namespace.
  2. Use it for manual checks and a few targeted E2E runs.
  3. Tear environments down automatically — zombie previews are how cloud bills invent folklore.
  4. Prefer the same deploy path as production, with smaller sizing.

Documentation-as-code per branch

Docs that live only on main lag reality. Build and publish documentation from the same branch as the change — preview sites, generated API refs, runbooks in the repo. We explored why this pattern wins in Documentation-as-Code Has Silently Won For Tech Content, and the same per-branch preview trick we used for GitLab Pages per Branch: The No-Compromise Hack to Serve Preview Pages is what makes the docs preview real on every MR.

Concrete:

  1. Keep docs in the repo next to the code they describe.
  2. Pipeline job: build docs on every branch; publish a per-branch preview (Pages, Storybook, OpenAPI UI…).
  3. Review doc diffs in the same MR as behavior changes.
  4. Link the preview URL in the MR description — reviewers should not need a séance to find the new endpoint.

Continuous delivery (always releasable + automated deploy)

Here we merge what tool vendors often split: continuous delivery means the software is always in a releasable state and the path to production is automated. Manual SSH snowflakes are not "careful"; they are unpaid drama. Continuous deployment (every green commit goes to prod) is optional once CD is real — a policy choice on top of the same machinery.

Concrete:

  1. One artifact promoted across environments; no "rebuild for prod."
  2. Deploy via pipeline or one approved click — identical steps every time.
  3. Keep main deployable; fixing releasability beats starting the next epic.
  4. Separate deploy from release with flags when the product is not ready for all users — this deploy/release decoupling use of flags is baseline; using flags to hide incomplete work behind trunk-based development is the elite form covered in section 5.
  5. Rehearse rollback / roll-forward on a boring Tuesday. (Friday deploys are fine when Tuesday already proved you can undo them.)

A pipeline you dare not touch is folklore, not automation — feed it continuously, as we argued in Keep Feeding Your CI/CD — Or Watch It Die.

Monitoring and observability

Daily deploys without eyes on production is Schrödinger's release: simultaneously fine and on fire until someone opens the dashboard.

Concrete:

  1. Track golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation.
  2. Structured logs with correlation IDs across services.
  3. Alert on actionable symptoms; paging for disk at 71% trains people to ignore the building on fire.
  4. Attach a runbook link to every alert that can wake a human.

Security shifted left

Security bolted on at the release CAB is how you discover CVEs during the demo. The cost of a finding grows roughly with the distance between where it was introduced and where it was caught — a vulnerable dependency caught in the MR is a version bump; the same dependency caught at the CAB is a release slip, and caught in production is an incident report. Shifting left is mostly an economic argument, not a moral one.

Concrete:

  1. Dependency and container scanning in CI.
  2. Secret detection on push.
  3. Threat-model new surfaces in the MR that introduces them.
  4. Fix criticals on a clock, not on vibes.

Simple design, refactoring, and managed debt

Craft is not a separate religion; it is how the baseline stays cheap over years.

Concrete:

  1. Boy-scout rule on touched files.
  2. Prefer delete over another abstract factory of abstract factories.
  3. Keep a visible debt list with cost-of-delay; budget a fixed capacity slice for structural work.
  4. Upgrade dependencies on a cadence before they become a liability.

4. Non-technical practices — elite

Elite culture and product habits turn a working pipeline into a learning system — the baseline ships reliably, these practices decide what gets shipped and whether the team survives shipping it. Skip them until the non-technical baseline is real; they are not a participation trophy.

Team experimentation and product hypotheses

Elite product management: try ideas without a twelve-signature approval pilgrimage.

Concrete:

  1. Frame work as hypotheses with kill criteria.
  2. Use flags and analytics to validate before scaling.
  3. Empower the team to run small experiments without leaving the team for permission.
  4. Celebrate killed experiments — they bought information cheaper than a full build.

Value-stream visibility

See the path from idea to production; attack waits, not only busy coding.

Concrete:

  1. Map the flow once; find the longest queue.
  2. Make blocked states visible on the board.
  3. Measure lead time by stage (code, review, QA, change board, prod).
  4. Optimize the bottleneck you measured, not the one that feels dramatic in standup.

Transformational leadership and wellbeing

Tools cannot compensate for a meat grinder. Leadership that enables learning, clarity, and sustainable pace shows up in delivery performance.

Concrete:

  1. Protect improvement time the same way you protect feature time.
  2. Remove approval steps that add delay without reducing risk.
  3. Watch burnout signals; hero culture is a leading indicator of outages.
  4. Hire and promote for teaching and collaboration, not only for lone-genius throughput.

5. Technical practices — elite

Baseline makes continuous delivery reachable. These practices remove remaining drag — adopt them when the baseline is already boringly reliable. Most teams should stay on the baseline longer than their slide deck suggests.

Trunk-based development and feature flags

Short-lived branches, frequent integration to trunk, incomplete work hidden behind flags. Powerful — and a mess if CI and tests are not trusted yet. The elite move here is TBD-driven flag usage: flags not just to decouple deploy from release (that is baseline), but to keep trunk always green while half-built features ship dark. See trunk-based development.

Concrete:

  1. Branch lifetime in hours/days, not weeks.
  2. Integrate to trunk at least daily.
  3. Feature flags for incomplete or risky exposure; product can toggle without a redeploy.
  4. Delete flags after rollout — flag archaeology is a special kind of haunted house.

Database change management

Schema changes are where "always releasable" goes to die if nobody owns the migration path.

Concrete:

  1. Migrations in version control, applied by the pipeline.
  2. Expand/contract for breaking changes; no dual-write hacks without a plan.
  3. Forward-only in production; rehearse rollback strategy when truly needed.
  4. Never "run this SQL from an email" as a release step.

Loosely coupled deployability

A team (or module) can deploy without a twelve-team release train. Note: a well-factored modular monolith is often the prerequisite that makes this decoupling reachable — splitting a tangled monolith into fashion microservices before you can deploy the monolith cleanly is a category error.

Concrete:

  1. Clear API contracts; version or expand carefully.
  2. Prefer a modular monolith before fashion microservices if you still have more services than users.
  3. Independent deploy pipelines per deployable unit.
  4. Contract tests between consumers and providers.

Advanced deployment strategies

When downtime or blast radius matters: blue/green, canary, dark launch. Feature flags often cover a surprising amount before you need full traffic-shifting machinery.

Concrete:

  1. Canary a percentage of traffic; watch error budgets before full rollout.
  2. Blue/green when you need instant cutover and easy revert.
  3. Dark launch: code live, users unaware — validate load before the marketing email.
  4. Automate the promotion criteria; humans confirm policy, not click fifty servers.

Internal platform and flexible infrastructure

Golden paths beat ticket queues — when the platform is a product, not a new bottleneck. Containers and IaC help reproducibility; they do not replace a green CI.

Concrete:

  1. Self-service: create preview env, run pipeline, deploy — without a week-long ticket.
  2. Infra-as-code for environments that matter.
  3. Autoscale runners and app capacity so branch previews do not block everyone else.
  4. Measure platform adoption and time-to-first-deploy for a new service.

6. Where to start (solo vs team)

Start with the non-technical baseline: small batches, stakeholder and user feedback, WIP. Pairing and generative collaboration when there is a second human. Without that loop, faster deploys just accelerate waste.

Solo — then the technical baseline, in roughly this order:

  1. Version control + CI on every branch (self-merged MRs are fine if CI is the gate).
  2. Modern testing strategy until the suite is trusted.
  3. Automated deploy path + monitoring (CD).
  4. Env + docs per branch when feedback before merge still hurts.
  5. Design / debt hygiene as a continuous tax.

Skip most of elite until this is dull.

Team with mandate — run non-technical and technical baselines in parallel. A collaborative team without CI is still slow; a perfect pipeline shipping the wrong thing is still waste.

Elite practices (product experimentation, value-stream mapping, TBD + flags, advanced deploys, platform) come after both baselines are dull. Trying trunk-based theatre on a flaky suite is how you invent new genres of merge conflict.

Wrapping up

Boring production is a stack, not a slogan. Split practices non-technical / technical, then baseline / elite — non-tech first because it prevails, elite last because it is not for everyone. Small batches, feedback, and WIP keep the loop pointed at value; pairing joins when there is a second human. A developer alone should then lean on the technical baseline: version, CI per branch, modern tests, CD with eyes on prod, docs and previews on the branch, craft that keeps the loop cheap — the pipeline is the other reviewer. Elite moves amplify a system that already works.

If you need one retro question: Which baseline practice — non-technical or technical — made boringly reliable, would shorten our path to valuable production most in the next ninety days? Fund that. Leave the Netflix costume in the closet.

articles.title: I spent 3.8 million tokens finding which service to change
articles.description: Code: github.com/alexcpn/catalogify · uv tool install catalogify · MIT  Take a monorepo with ninety...
articles.body_html:
Code: github.com/alexcpn/catalogify · uv tool install catalogify · MIT

Take a monorepo with ninety microservices in it. A spec lands that will touch maybe three of them. Before anyone writes code, somebody has to work out which three, and on a repo that size that is most of the job.

I wanted to know what it costs to let an agent answer that. So I did the obvious thing and gave it a map.

There are good tools for this now. I used Graphify, which parses your code with tree-sitter and builds a queryable graph of every symbol and call edge. It runs locally, needs no API key, and tags every edge with whether it was extracted or inferred. I pointed it at one service and it chewed through 706 files in twenty seconds.

Then I looked at what it produced.

graph.json, 14.5 MB. About 3.8 million tokens for one service.

Ten candidate services would be 38 million. Ninety would be 343 million. And routing is a comparison problem, so you can't just load the winner. You have to load everything you're choosing between.

That was the moment I realised I'd been solving the wrong problem.

Two questions, opposite shapes

There are two questions people lump together as "give the agent context on the codebase."

Which service does this touch? Wide and shallow. You need a little about everything.

Inside that service, what changes? Narrow and deep. You need everything about a little.

Graphify is superb at the second one. graphify affected "UpdateApiUsageCount" --depth 2 gives you a precise impact radius in a few hundred tokens. Nothing I write by hand will ever beat that, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

But the artifact backing those queries has to be complete, and completeness is exactly the wrong property for the first question. You're not asking about symbols. You're asking which service owns pod eviction, or image pulls, or volume mounting, and a call graph doesn't know that, because ownership isn't a topological fact.

You can see it in the filenames. Graphify will export a markdown wiki, which is the right instinct. For one service it wrote 446 articles called things like basicWorkQueue.md and allPrimitiveFieldPaths.md. Those are symbols, clustered by how tightly the code couples. Useful for tracing. Useless for picking a service.

What the opposite costs

So I built the other thing. One small markdown file per service, in the language the spec is written in, with typed frontmatter and links to its neighbours.

For the same Kubernetes component, same 108,648 lines of Go:

Size Tokens
Structural graph 14.5 MB 3,813,486
Its markdown wiki 1,004 KB 256,968
One service entry 2.6 KB 676

Ninety of those is 61,000 tokens. That fits in one cheap call with the spec still sitting next to it.

The part that surprised me

I wrote the generator to mine git history, on a hunch that the interesting stuff lives in reverts. Then I ran it against the kubelet's container manager and got this back:

508709d007e  cpumanager: improve V4 checkpoint corruption error
bc752cdfdb0  Fix V3 checkpoint checksum for rollback compatibility
76100602564  Revert "Fix CPU checkpoint migration V2 to V3"

Chase that revert to the commit it reverted and the story comes out. When a V3 checkpoint has a bad checksum, restore falls back to V2, but the V3 fields it already read stay in the struct. You get a hybrid. Someone fixed that, and the fix got reverted, so it may still be sitting there.

Nobody wrote that in a comment. There's no ADR. It exists in the commit log and in the head of whoever was on call that week.

That's the stuff I actually want in a routing catalog, and it's the stuff no parser can reach, because the engineer fixing production at 2am was not writing documentation.

Peter Naur got here in 1985. His argument in Programming as Theory Building is that the real product of programming is the theory of the system carried in the developers' heads, not the code, and that no amount of program text or documentation carries it for them. A program whose original team has dispersed is, in his word, dead. A new team patching a dead program makes fixes that look fine locally and quietly wreck the design.

That is the position an AI agent is in on its first commit to your repository. It arrives after the team dispersed, holding the artifacts and none of the theory, and it patches with total confidence.

Writing a better spec does not get you out of it. Brooks settled that one: the complexity of software is essential rather than accidental, so descriptions that abstract it away abstract away the essence. The ceiling is the same whether a human or a model wrote the spec.

A revert is not the theory. It is a fossil of one place where the theory and the code collided hard enough that somebody had to act at speed. Fossils are cheap to collect, and they are worth more than anything else in the catalog.

What I'd do instead

Two layers, and let each tool do the thing it's good at.

Route with markdown. Small files, domain language, one per service, cheap enough to read all of them.

Reach with the graph. Run it inside the one service you picked, call it as a CLI, keep graph.json in .gitignore and out of your context window entirely.

The composition costs less than either half does alone once you're past a few dozen services.

One more thing, since I'd rather say it than have it found: the first time I ran my own tool against Kubernetes it crashed. Exit 141. A head -N closing a pipe under set -o pipefail, which never fires on a small repo because the producer finishes writing before head walks away. Every test I'd written passed. If you only test on small repos, you're only testing the easy case.

Fixed, measured, and the numbers above are all reproducible:

uv tool install catalogify
catalogify install

Then ask your agent for a knowledge bundle. On a monorepo, start coarse.

Source and issues: github.com/alexcpn/catalogify.

Package: pypi.org/project/catalogify.

For Spec Kit projects the same workflows ship as slash commands in speckit_okf.

It is a few days old and I would rather hear where it breaks than where it shines.

MIT licensed. Measurements against kubernetes/kubernetes at d5ccf7968e5, tokens estimated at bytes ÷ 4. The comparison tool is Graphify, run AST-only without an API key.

articles.title: Prompting Will Be Dead in Six Months
articles.description: That's at least what every tech bro is saying right now on Twitter.  The next wave, apparently, is...
articles.body_html:
That's at least what every tech bro is saying right now on Twitter.

The next wave, apparently, is graph engineering.

Okay, So What the Heck Is Graph Engineering?

If you picture a normal AI agent, it's typically one model looping through an entire task by itself, over and over, until it decides, yeah, this is good enough.

Graph engineering breaks that into smaller pieces called nodes.

A node is just one specific job, a researcher, a writer, or a fact checker. Each has its own model call or its own agent.

Nodes connect through edges, and an edge decides what happens next based on what the last node just did.

So say, for example, the fact checker finds an error. The edge flags it and sends the task back to the writer node with the error attached, so the writer knows exactly what to fix. Only once the fact checker approves it does the edge let the work move forward.

That's the core of graph engineering.

My Take

It's not really a new discipline. It's the same orchestration that myself and other people have been doing with tools like LangGraph for over a year, with a little sprinkle on it.

The term just went viral this month. But before it, it was loop engineering. Before that, harness engineering. Before that, context engineering.

Same idea, just slight changes. And every time, someone keeps declaring the old term dead when really it just got a slight improvement.

So No, Prompting Isn't Dying in Six Months

What's actually dying is the idea that you can duct tape one model to one clever prompt and call it a finished agentic system.

Follow and I'll keep you posted.
